channel: Oil volumes and export routes
quantified: Budget assumes real GDP +10.9% in 2027 after -2.1% in 2026; oil activity -14.6% through Q3 2026; Saudi crude ~9.2–10.6 mb/d in Oct 2026 vs 6.8 mb/d in Q2.
rationale: The final budget's growth path rests on oil output recovering from the 2026 disruption (Minister: higher Q4 output raises the 2027 base). For the sector this means higher volumes in 2027 than in 2026, but also less of the crisis price premium that lifted 9M 2026 revenue. Our 9M 2026 split for Aramco shows price added about +13 pp and volume took about −10 pp, so a reversal of both would roughly offset in revenue terms. The net effect is therefore uncertain in sign, though large in size.
depends_on_execution: Security of Hormuz and Red Sea shipping; OPEC+ 2027 levels set on 29 Nov 2026
risks: Renewed attacks on facilities or shipping; faster price normalisation than volume recovery
indicators_to_watch: Monthly Saudi output (OPEC secondary sources and direct communication); Brent; OPEC+ 29 Nov decision; Hormuz traffic

channel: Oil volumes, prices and export capacity
quantified: 9M 2026: realised crude +29.2% ($91.7 vs $71.0), liquids output −15.2%; crude revenue +7.6%.
rationale: Aramco carries almost all the sector's exposure to the volume/price swing described in P-E-01. The budget does not publish an oil-revenue assumption for 2027, so the fiscal plan cannot be read across to Aramco's revenue. The Energy Minister's plan to lift East-West Pipeline throughput to about 10 mb/d would reduce dependence on Hormuz. It is a statement of intent with no final investment decision, so its revenue effect is not determinable.
depends_on_execution: Pipeline expansion is a stated plan without FID; budget gives no 2027 oil revenue figure
risks: Lower prices as supply returns; capex for resilience
indicators_to_watch: Aramco Q4 2026/FY2026 realised price and production; EWP project FID

channel: Government funding needs and dividends
quantified: Deficit SAR 190.6bn (3.6% of GDP); debt to SAR 1,923bn; financing expenses +31.1% to SAR 93bn. Aramco 2025 dividends paid SAR 320.4bn vs FY2025 free cash flow SAR 320.4bn (our calculation).
rationale: A wider deficit and rising interest costs keep the state reliant on Aramco's base dividend (+3.5% a year per company policy). No budget document or ministerial statement announces a change to Aramco's dividend. We treat continued dividend dependence as a constraint on Aramco's capital allocation, not as a measure.
depends_on_execution: No announced change; depends on future company/shareholder decisions
risks: Payout pressure while capex stays at USD 50–55bn
indicators_to_watch: Aramco dividend declarations; any government share sale

channel: Domestic energy prices and subsidies
quantified: Subsidies fall 61.6% to SAR 18bn; electricity and water tariffs rise from 1 Jan 2027; diesel SAR 1.79/l in 2026 (from 0.63 in 2022).
rationale: The confirmed tariff reform applies to electricity and water. Aramco's domestic fuel and feedstock prices are set separately and are not changed by the budget. Higher regulated prices would raise Aramco's domestic revenue but reduce the government's price-equalisation compensation (other income related to sales), so the net effect is small. Further fuel-price moves would need separate announcements.
depends_on_execution: Further fuel/feedstock price announcements (not in the budget)
indicators_to_watch: Annual fuel and feedstock price notices (January); other income related to sales

channel: Shipping demand, freight rates and security
quantified: Bahri 9M 2026 revenue SAR 26.1bn vs 7.1bn (SAR 20.9bn from Aramco); VLCC time-charter rates above USD 1m/day in Sep 2026.
rationale: Bahri's 2026 surge came from crisis freight rates and Aramco's rerouted exports. The budget's normalisation scenario (restored oil flows) implies more cargo but lower rates, and rate normalisation would dominate. The government marine-insurance pool (cutting insurance costs by 50–60%) is a confirmed support measure that lowers Bahri's costs while risk persists. The Houthi blockade of Saudi shipping and the attack on its tanker AMZAN show the security risk is company-specific.
depends_on_execution: Duration of the conflict premium; Red Sea security
indicators_to_watch: VLCC TCE rates (TD3C); Bahri Q4 2026 results; Red Sea incidents

channel: Refining margins, utility tariffs and shareholder support
quantified: Petro Rabigh 9M 2026 net profit SAR 6.7bn vs a SAR 3.3bn loss; industrial electricity tariff 23 halalas/kWh from 2027.
rationale: The 2026 profit came from crisis refining margins, which are not a budget item. As supply normalises those margins are likely to narrow. The confirmed tariff increase adds a modest cost. Shareholder support from Aramco (about 60%) remains the key funding backstop.
depends_on_execution: Margin outlook not in any official document
indicators_to_watch: Product cracks; Petro Rabigh Q4 2026

channel: Upstream drilling activity and financing costs
quantified: ADES: offshore rigs suspended in 2026 with about SAR 140m non-recurring effect; notices to resume two Saudi offshore rigs; 9M 2026 finance costs SAR 976m vs 668m.
rationale: Restored output and the gas programme (Jafurah, Tanajib) support rig demand in 2027. Maximum sustainable capacity is held at 12 mb/d, which limits new oil-capacity drilling. Higher policy rates (SAMA +25 bp in Sep 2026) and the government's focus on domestic borrowing raise funding costs for a leveraged driller.
depends_on_execution: Rig resumption notices; Aramco upstream programme
indicators_to_watch: Aramco rig resumptions; ADES backlog; SAIBOR

channel: Upstream drilling activity and refinancing
quantified: Arabian Drilling FY2025 net loss SAR 75m; offshore rigs suspended from end-Mar 2026; SAR 2bn sukuk due Feb 2027; covenant breach waived (filings).
rationale: The same activity channel as ADES applies. The refinancing need is more pressing here: a SAR 2bn sukuk matures in Feb 2027 while banks face tighter funding and government borrowing competes for domestic liquidity. The impact depends on rig resumptions and on refinancing terms.
depends_on_execution: Refinancing of the Feb 2027 sukuk; rig resumptions
indicators_to_watch: Sukuk refinancing announcement; rig count

channel: Equity-market and portfolio exposure
quantified: SARCO results are driven by dividends and its listed-share portfolio.
rationale: SARCO has no direct budget channel. Wider foreign access to listed shares (from 1 Feb 2026) affects its portfolio only through market prices.
indicators_to_watch: TASI performance

channel: Government borrowing and bank liquidity
quantified: 2026: SAR 298bn raised to Q3, 79% domestic (≈ SAR 235bn, about 7.6% of bank deposits of SAR 3,076bn — our calculation). 2027: deficit SAR 190.6bn, with borrowing to 'focus on domestic and private market channels'; the 2027 borrowing plan is not yet published.
rationale: This is a confirmed financing strategy. The government will keep drawing on domestic savings, while bank loans already exceed customer deposits (simple loan-to-deposit ratio 107% at 30 Sep 2026, our data). Fitch reports funding has become tighter and more expensive, and time and savings deposits now exceed demand deposits. The Finance Minister says he wants to avoid crowding out private borrowers, which is a signal rather than a measure. J.P. Morgan index inclusion of SAR government sukuk from 29 Jan 2027 should bring foreign buyers and ease some of the pressure.
depends_on_execution: Size and mix of the 2027 borrowing plan (not yet published)
opportunities: Higher yields on sukuk holdings; index-driven foreign demand
indicators_to_watch: NDMC 2027 borrowing plan; monthly SAR sukuk auctions; 3M SAIBOR; time-deposit share

channel: Government spending and project lending
quantified: 2027 spending SAR 1,392bn, −3% vs the 2026 estimate; capex SAR 178bn (−2.1%); municipal services +12%; general items incl. a mega-projects allocation +6%; infrastructure & transport −7%.
rationale: The final budget trims total and capital spending. The Finance Minister also speaks of rescheduling and restructuring some projects, which is a signal and not quantified. Both point to slower project and contractor lending after loan growth of about 12% a year in 2022–2025 (our data). Fitch expects sector credit growth of about 8% in 2027.
indicators_to_watch: Quarterly budget capex; project awards; corporate loan growth

channel: Contractor payments and credit quality
quantified: New Government Tenders and Procurement Law requires private-sector dues to be paid within set timeframes before new commitments.
rationale: This is a confirmed legal change. It should reduce payment delays to contractors, a recurring source of working-capital stress and impairments in bank corporate books.
indicators_to_watch: Corporate impairment charges

channel: Interest rates
quantified: SAMA raised repo to 4.50% on 16 Sep 2026 (after cuts to 4.25%); demand deposits are 66% of SNB's and 59% of Al Rajhi's customer deposits, but 17% at SAIB and 23% at Bank Aljazira.
rationale: Higher policy rates help banks funded largely by non-interest-bearing demand deposits and hurt those that rely on term deposits. Our data show margin-on-assets compression at SAIB (2.7% to 2.1%) and Bank Aljazira (2.4% to 1.9%) between FY2022 and FY2025. This is not a budget measure; SAMA follows the US Federal Reserve under the riyal peg.
indicators_to_watch: SAMA decisions; 3M SAIBOR

channel: Household support, tariffs and retail credit
quantified: SANED wage support (3 months), Citizen Account extended to end-2027, SAR 500 monthly allowance increase; electricity/water tariffs up from 1 Jan 2027; new mortgages −12% in 2025.
rationale: Confirmed support measures cushion household incomes during the disruption, while the tariff increases raise living costs. Housing measures (the Riyadh rent freeze, the land release, and property ownership for non-Saudis from 22 Jan 2026) have coincided with slower new mortgage lending. Retail-heavy banks are most exposed.
indicators_to_watch: Monthly new mortgages; retail impairments

channel: Capital requirements
quantified: Countercyclical buffer 1% of risk-weighted assets from 25 May 2026; listed banks issued about SAR 34.5bn of mostly AT1 sukuk in 2026 to 19 Sep.
rationale: This is a confirmed measure. Banks are meeting it partly with Tier 1 sukuk, whose distributions reduce returns to ordinary shareholders. That effect is already visible in rising Tier 1 balances in our data.
indicators_to_watch: Tier 1 issuance; CET1 ratios
